items.body:
In her speech to the CBI, Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, delivered one of the most detailed explanations we have had from a minister as to what Andy Burnham means when he calls for more public control of utilities.

She said that the government was not against markets, and that in areas like telecoms privatisation had worked. But in water and energy it hadn’t, she insisted. She suggested that, in wanting more public control in these sectors, the government was aligned with the US, “hardly a hotbed of state socialism”.

She said:

Now I know the word privatisation can start an argument. So let me be precise. This is not about whether markets work. They do. Where there is genuine competition, as in telecoms, markets have given consumers choice and kept prices low while delivering infrastructure.
The social licence to operate must be won every day by building trust and having the best value, product or service. Where competition exists, it should be left to thrive, supported by our strong, independent Competition and Markets Authority.
But when it comes to essential services, we have spent four decades trying and failing to recreate market conditions when consumers have no alternative.
Public control is about getting the right outcomes. It’s not ideological. Ownership is not a requirement. We took the railway back into public ownership because it wasn’t working for passengers or the taxpayer. But we want Great British Railways to be challenged by open access operators in Greater Manchester’s Bee Network, which you may have heard of. Routes are set by the elected mayor to benefit the community. The services are still run by private operators.
Delivering the homes we need depends on a buoyant developer sector.
Looking at water and energy, we must accept that the status quo is not the neutral, pragmatic, centre ground. It’s the outlier, an exception that no other nation is trying to emulate.
Around the world, the core infrastructure of water overwhelmingly stays in public hands. England is almost unique in handing the entire system to private owners. The only other country in that corner with us is Chile.
We are also one of the few countries in Europe whose electricity and gas transmission networks are entirely privately owned. And here’s the irony. Foreign governments now own a bigger share of our utilities than the British government does – significant stakes in our water, electricity and gas networks, returns paid to their taxpayers.
I welcome that investment. Let me be clear about that. But it raises a question: why do other governments see the strategic and commercial value in holding Britain’s essential assets, when for 40 years the British government couldn’t?
And it isn’t just Europe. Look at the United States of America, hardly a hotbed of state socialism. Most Americans get their water from a public utility. Fewer than one in 10 get it from a private one. Community-owned power companies serve one in seven American electricity customers in Los Angeles and Seattle, in Nashville, in Austin, and the federal government still owns the Tennessee Valley Authority, one of the biggest power companies in the country. Nobody thinks America is anti-business.
So let’s be honest with ourselves. The status quo is the ideological position, and saying so should not be taboo.

Haigh also said that past governments had resorted to trying to make the privatisation of utilities work through excessive regulation.

To make the experiment work, successive governments leant on regulation, first to try to recreate competition from monopolies through a spreadsheet; then to manage what private markets would never price on their own, like the spare capacity that keeps the lights on; then to deliver social policy, treated as a free good because it went on the bill, not the budget.
Ofgem now has six times the staff it had in the early 2000s, almost three times the administrative budget in real terms, and a rule book more than six times longer. We’ve got a hulking, complex behemoth of a regulatory state. It satisfies no one. Not consumers, not investors. When you prioritise everything, you prioritise nothing.
In the fog of complexity, bad actors can thrive, while the rest of us can’t move with a clarity and pace this moment demands.
That is why public control should not alarm anyone in this room. It’s not ideological. It’s pragmatic, and it’s essential – for people, for places, and for business.
We will measure our progress against three tests: affordability, investability, accountability.

Louise Haigh at the CBI. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA

items.title: Flights and train services cancelled in Belgium due to strike
items.summary: A series of strikes have hit Belgium in recent months as the prime minister struggles to agree a budget to cut costs.
items.body:
Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Brussels Airport is receiving no travellers until 21:00 on Monday

ByPaulin Kola

Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and train services have been severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.

All air traffic has been halted in Zaventem airport in the capital, Brussels, as well as Charlerois, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.

Trains and underground services have also been halted in Brussels where large numbers of people are expected to join a protest march.

The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever has so far failed to agree a budget to cut costs with his coalition allies. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.

No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers. More than 50,000 travellers' plans were being disrupted - with more expected to be affected overnight and on Tuesday.

A similar situation has affected Charlerois, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure of arrival.

"Without air traffic control, no flights can take off or land," the airport said on Saturday when the strike action was announced, warning of "disastrous consequences".

As thousands descended on Brussels for the protest march, the leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".

"A genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes," Bert Engelaar, head of FGBT, said.

"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," Engelaar said, praising the left-wing Vooruit party - the only member of the five-party governing coalition reported to have stalled efforts to agree the budget.

Vooruit wants to raise taxes on the rich, and fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.

Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.

Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.

items.title: Mexican soldiers attacked in wake of drug lord's arrest
items.summary: Eight suspects are arrested after firing on soldiers trying to re-establish order following the arrest of 'El Chapo Isidro'.
items.body:
Image source, Daniel Cardenas/Anadolu via Getty Images

Image caption,

Extra forces have been deployed to guard the facility where 'Chapo Isidro' is in custody

ByVanessa Buschschlüter

Latin America online editor

Mexican soldiers have detained eight alleged members of a drug cartel whose leader was arrested on Friday, sparking a wave of violence in northern Sinaloa state.

The Mexican defence ministry said the soldiers were shot by the suspects on Sunday while on patrol in the town of Sinaloa de Leyva, trying to re-establish order in the wake of the arrest of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores.

Meza Flores, also known as "Chapo Isidro", was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list and had managed to evade capture for years.

The ministry said the eight had also been involved in the retaliatory violence unleashed by Meza Flores's cartel in the hours after his arrest on Friday.

In a statement published on social media, external, the ministry of defence said that one of the detainees was under age.

It added that its special forces had seized six vehicles as part of their operation, two of which had been fitted with bullet-proof armour and gun turrets.

The US Department of Justice described Friday's arrest of Meza Flores as "a spectacular military operation" and congratulated Mexico's military and special forces on his capture.

It said that the US Homeland Security Task Force had supported the Mexican military and praised the "bilateral effort".

Figure caption,

Watch: Suspected drug lord 'El Chapo Isidro' transferred to Mexico's capital

Mexico's defence ministry said its special forces had used stealth and surprise to reach the home of the wanted man.

They also established a security perimeter to prevent Meza Flores from escaping and cartel reinforcements from arriving.

Nevertheless, a bloody firefight ensued.

Along with Meza Flores, his second-in-command, known as "Serafín", and his financial operator, were also arrested and quickly transferred by air to Mexico City.

As news of their arrest spread, members of their cartel erected barricades on major roads and set cars and some shops alight.

There were also reports of shoot-outs between the security forces and cartel members.

The prosecutor's office in Sinaloa says 17 people, four of them members of the Mexican security forces, were killed as a result of the violence on Friday and early Saturday.

Who is 'Chapo Isidro'?

US Assistant Attorney General A Tysen Duva has described Meza Flores as "the most dangerous man in Mexico".

"For decades Meza Flores has promoted the terrorist objectives of the Sinaloa cartel," Duva said, accusing him of "flooding the United States with deadly substances".

The 44-year-old is believed to have started his criminal career with the Juárez cartel decades ago.

He later moved on to become the right-hand man of the leader of the Beltrán Leyva Organisation, a drug gang once allied to the Sinaloa cartel before the two groups split and became bitter enemies.

As early as 2013, the US Treasury identified Meza Flores as the leader of his own drug-trafficking organisation, named after him.

The US Treasury said at the time, that the Meza Flores drug trafficking organisation was responsible for "the distribution of large quantities of methamphetamine, heroin, marijuana, and cocaine to the United States".

It added that the turf war between the Meza Flores cartel and the Sinaloa cartel had "resulted in the quadrupling of drug-war killings" in between 2009 and 2013.

According to think tank Insight Crime, external, Meza Flores himself kept a low profile over the last decade while continuing to run his cartel out of Guasave, in Sinaloa state.

The head of the US Drug Enforcement Administration said that his capture was a "significant blow to a ruthless criminal organisation that has used extreme violence to traffic deadly drugs, including fentanyl, a designated weapon of mass destruction, into American communities".

His arrest, and the co-operation between US and Mexican officials which led to it, will be seen as a win for the government of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum.

Sheinbaum has stressed that she is keen to work with the US authorities to capture high-profile target as long as Mexican's sovereignty is respected.

items.title: Democrats reveal details for 2028 presidential primary after midterm victories – US politics live
items.summary: Party says there will be 12 debates to select a candidate from what is expected to be a large number of hopefuls Sign up to the Breaking News US email Donald Trump is scheduled to deliver remarks at the Department of Justice this afternoon, officially billed as “Remarks on Protecting American Famili…
items.body:
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Democrats are planning 12 presidential primary debates for what’s expected to be a crowded field of 2028 candidates, with the first scheduled for June, the Democratic National Committee has said.

The DNC’s announcement on Monday comes before major candidates have launched campaigns to succeed term-limited Republican president Donald Trump and follows the party’s convincing midterm performance, AP reported.

DNC Chairman Ken Martin said in a statement the party is aimed at staying united and helping the eventual nominee win the White House. “The DNC is keeping our foot on the gas as we head into the 2028 cycle,” he said.

Anticipating a large number of presidential hopefuls, the DNC said it will cap participation in each debate to 20 qualifying candidates over two nights, if needed.

The criteria for making the debate stage will be similar to 2020, when there was also a big field and a dozen debates, the DNC said, and will include meeting polling and other criteria such as grassroots fundraising.

More details are set to be announced in January, including specific times and locations for the debates, the DNC said, though the party confirmed that five debates will be in 2027 and seven in 2028. The final primary debate is planned for March 2028.

For the first time, candidates must pledge to reject dark money as a condition of making the debate stage. The new requirement is part of a ​DNC effort to curb the influence of outside groups that can spend unlimited amounts to support or oppose candidates without having to reveal funding sources.

The debate schedule is one of the most closely watched decisions the DNC makes, along with selecting the city for the 2028 convention. Earlier this year, the DNC narrowed the list of cities to Boston, Denver and Philadelphia.

In other developments:

• Donald Trump has headlined his third cryptocurrency gala at his ​country club in Virginia, rewarding top holders of his own meme coin, as Democrats accuse the president of improperly profiting from his crypto ventures. The dinner, which took place at the Trump National golf club in Sterling, Virginia, included meet-and-greets with Trump supporters including the boxing champion Floyd Mayweather, the Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary, the NBA champion Tristan Thompson and the magician Lior Suchard, according to the event’s website.

• Michigan US senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday doubled down on naming healthcare reform legislation after Donald Trump as long as it meant the president would not impede its passage. “If he’s open to the conversation, I am open to it, too,” El-Sayed said of Trump on Sunday. “If the president is opening to signing that bill, let’s get it done.”

• Jay Clayton, the US director of national intelligence, said he trusts Trump “completely” after the US president called Vladimir Putin “a friend” during their recent meeting in China. Clayton made the remarks on Sunday, where he was pressed during media appearances on Trump’s warm characterization of the Russian president – who is viewed as a chief US adversary – following his trilateral summit with Putin and China’s Xi Jinping.

• Invoking Greek mythology, US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”. The Louisiana Republican’s allusion to the legendary figure whose desirability was such that it caused the mythic Trojan war came during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday.

• Democrats have won their largest majority in the House in more than three decades after Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina on Sunday, extending the blue wave that swept the US midterms and increasing pressure on the party to deliver its promises to US voters. House Democrats have secured at least 258 seats in a midterm election sweep unseen since 1992, gaining 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in Donald Trump’s first midterm in 2018.

items.title: Environment Agency and Natural England face axe in Labour quango cull
items.summary: Louise Haigh says the two environmental regulators are being reviewed as part of shake-up of arm’s length bodies Ministers are considering abolishing two of England’s biggest environmental regulators in an attempt to give politicians greater control over what gets built and where. Louise Haigh, the…
items.body:
A badger sett in Hambledon, Surrey. Haigh did not push back against the idea Natural England was being targeted for abolition. Photograph: Lillian King/Getty Images

A badger sett in Hambledon, Surrey. Haigh did not push back against the idea Natural England was being targeted for abolition. Photograph: Lillian King/Getty Images

Natural England could be abolished as part of quango cull, says Louise Haigh

First secretary of state says proliferation of arms-length government bodies is hampering decision-making

The nature watchdog Natural England could be abolished as part of a cull of arm’s length government organisations, Louise Haigh has said.

Saying that the proliferation of quangos and other similar bodies had made decision-making by ministers more difficult, the first secretary of state said it could fall within a push to change the landscape of government by scrapping some organisations and bringing others into departments.

Abolishing Natural England could be justified on the basis that it could speed up planning decisions and thus boost housebuilding and growth, but removing or curbing its role would be likely to prompt concern from environmental groups.

Last month, the Conservatives announced that if they won power they would abolish both Natural England and the Environment Agency, saying this would help create more new homes.

items.summary: Decision to deny visas to more than 60 students overturned after high court orders justice department to reconsider Twenty students from Gaza are to travel to Ireland to take up scholarships after winning a battle for visas that undercut the Irish government’s reputation as a champion of Palestinian…
items.body:
Decision to deny visas dismayed opposition politicians and other critics who accused government of betraying Ireland’s record of solidarity with Palestinians. Photograph: Emilija Jefremova/Reuters

Decision to deny visas dismayed opposition politicians and other critics who accused government of betraying Ireland’s record of solidarity with Palestinians. Photograph: Emilija Jefremova/Reuters

Students from Gaza win visa battle to study in Ireland

Decision to deny visas to more than 60 students overturned after high court orders justice department to reconsider

Twenty students from Gaza are to travel to Ireland to take up scholarships after winning a battle for visas that undercut the Irish government’s reputation as a champion of Palestinians.

The group is due to leave the territory on Monday under strict Israeli controls and travel via Jordan to Dublin to take up places at Irish universities. Another group is expected to follow next month.

The evacuation comes after a four-month campaign to overturn a decision by the Irish Department of Justice to deny visas to more than 60 students in Gaza who had been offered scholarships in Ireland.

The decision dismayed opposition politicians and other critics who accused the department of betraying Ireland’s record of solidarity with Palestinians.

The government backed down last week after a Dublin high court ordered the department to reconsider the decision. The minister for justice, Jim O’Callaghan, approved 48 visas. The first group is expected to arrive on Tuesday, with the remainder coming in late December.

“It’s a mix of feelings I still can’t fully describe,” Amir Alareer, 26, who is to study cybersecurity and artificial intelligence at University College Dublin, said via email on the eve of his departure from Gaza.

“There is hope and relief after months of waiting and fighting for this moment. But it is hard to feel complete joy when I am leaving my family behind in Gaza, and when 28 of my fellow students, who hold the same visas and share the same dreams, are still here waiting.”

The students originally expected to come in summer, and had supporting paperwork from Irish universities, but in July the Department of Justice rejected the visa applications. “The refusals hit us hard,” said Alareer.

The department demanded bank statements, proof of intention to return and other documents and said any appeal would have to be made by post, saying screening and verification were integral to the immigration system.

The students said such documents had not previously been requested and that Gaza’s banking and postal service had been destroyed. Ivana Bacik, a legislator and leader of the Labour party, accused the department of using “spurious reasons” amid a hardening of immigration policy.

Alareer helped to lead a campaign from Gaza that was backed in Ireland by demonstrators, a petition and an open letter signed by actors, writers and artists including Hozier, Nicola Coughlan and the rap group Kneecap. “Running a campaign from Gaza, through blackouts and displacement, was not easy, but I knew that if we stayed silent, our case would be forgotten,” said Alareer.

In October, the high court ruled that there were “significant and demonstrable errors” in the refusal of a visa to Shaymaa Abudalu, a 20-year-old who had been offered an engineering scholarship at University College Cork, and who was the lead case in a batch of similar lawsuits. A high court judge welcomed the decision last week to grant 48 visas and said “huge progress” had been made.

Among the students are five members of a dance troupe who have been offered places at the Irish World Academy of Music and Dance at the University of Limerick.

Alareer, who studied engineering at Al-Azhar University – Gaza, said Israel’s attacks on Gaza had destroyed his home and displaced the family several times. “The hardest experience of all was the famine, when we couldn’t find even a single kilo of flour.” Floods have impeded recent relief efforts.

His family was proud of his scholarship, he said, but saying goodbye would be hard. “They are happy that I finally have this opportunity, but leaving them behind after everything we have been through together is incredibly difficult.”

After studying software and innovation in Dublin, Alareer plans to return to Al-Azhar University and establish a cybersecurity department. “I want to build a generation of Palestinian engineers and researchers who can protect our digital future. Gaza will be rebuilt, and its systems must be rebuilt securely, by its own people.”

items.title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 after flipping North Carolina seat
items.summary: Democrats have now won at least 258 seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats.
items.body:
Image source, Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images

Image caption,

Chuck Hubbard is a former journalist whose first political campaign was in 2022

ByMadeline Halpert

The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.

The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.

The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.

Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.

• View the 2026 midterm election results

Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.

She conceded on Sunday, saying in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."

Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images

Image caption,

Virginia Foxx spent a decade in the North Carolina Senate before representing the state in the House of Representatives

Hubbard, meanwhile, wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".

He added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."

Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.

Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.

President Donald Trump himself has suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses, as well as Vice President JD Vance.

Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.

The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.

Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law.

However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

items.summary: Authorities say they believe the Saturday night shooting at a concert in Strathmore ‘may be gang-related’ Nine people were shot at a concert in central California , leaving one person critically injured with a chest injury, the local sheriff said Sunday. The shooting broke out at about 7.30pm Saturd…
items.body:
The shooting broke out Saturday night at a concert attended by about 150 people in Strathmore, authorities said. Photograph: Matt Rourke/AP

The shooting broke out Saturday night at a concert attended by about 150 people in Strathmore, authorities said. Photograph: Matt Rourke/AP

Nine people shot at central California concert with one in critical condition

Authorities say they believe the Saturday night shooting at a concert in Strathmore ‘may be gang-related’

Nine people were shot at a concert in central California, leaving one person critically injured with a chest injury, the local sheriff said Sunday.

The shooting broke out at about 7.30pm Saturday at a concert attended by about 150 people in Strathmore, a small town in Tulare county, a mountainous region in the center of the state, the local sheriff’s department said in a statement. An unspecified number of suspects opened fire on the crowd. No arrests were announced.

One 26-year-old man was shot in the chest and required surgery. He remained in critical condition, the sheriff’s department said. Two other victims ages 19 and 22 also required surgery, while six people sustained minor injuries.

Authorities said that they believe the shooting “may be gang-related” but didn’t elaborate. The show in the town of roughly 3,000 people featured performers from neighboring states, the department said.

The department didn’t immediately respond to emailed questions seeking further details but said there was no longer any immediate threat to the public.

As of Monday, there had been more than 420 mass shootings in the US so far for the year, according to the Gun Violence Archive. The archive, a nonpartisan resources, defines mass shootings as cases in which four or more victims are either wounded or killed.

High numbers of mass shootings reported annually in the US have prompted many to call for more substantial federal gun control. But Congress over the years has not passed such restrictions.

items.title: Presidential villa suffers water and power cuts, Nigerian leader says
items.summary: Bola Tinubu says he was shaving last week when the water cut out - an experience familiar to many Nigerians.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Tinubu made the disclosure at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family

ByMansur Abubakar

Reporting fromAbuja

Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu says the presidential villa suffers from cuts in electricity and water - failures that plague ordinary citizens.

He said he was shaving last week when the water supply at the villa, known as Aso Rock, in Abuja cut.

He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to address these issues..

Tinubu made the disclosure on Sunday at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family in Lagos.

He explained: "On the Wednesday of last week, I was shaving, and the water went off. In the villa, you won't know punishment dey dia too [there’s punishment there too in Nigerian pidgin].

"The water went off. So we will correct all this. No light, no water, no electricity, no development. We have just started. We can do it, and we will do it for Nigeria,” he said.

Aso Villa serves as both the office and official residence of the Nigerian president. It is situated at the base of Aso Rock in Abuja.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Many Nigerians rely on generators like these to power their homes and businesses

Nigeria has long endured electricity shortages, but recent severe disruptions have been caused primarily by insufficient gas supplies and declining hydropower output, rather than the usual nationwide grid collapse.

Persistent blackouts in Lagos, Abuja and elsewhere have forced distribution companies to implement rotating power cuts, severely impacting households and businesses.

The country also suffers from chronic water shortages, the result of a structural crisis rooted in the gap between rapid urban population growth and decaying, inadequate public water infrastructure.

Tinubu made a high-profile electricity promise during the 2023 election campaign, but the exact wording and how binding it is has become a major point of contention ahead of the 16 January election.

Tinubu defeated the country’s former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as well as Peter Obi in 2023 and the three are seen as the strongest contenders once again.

items.summary: Tata-owned Agratas plant to build EV batteries for sister company Jaguar Land Rover seen as crucial for long-term health of British car industry One of the UK’s flagship electric vehicle battery projects has been thrown into turmoil after its second building contractor in five months walked away, ad…
items.body:
The Freelander 8, the first Freelander-branded electric vehicle jointly developed by British carmaker Jaguar Land Rover and Chinese joint-venture partner Chery displayed at a launch event in Wuhu, China. Photograph: Nick Carey/Reuters

The Freelander 8, the first Freelander-branded electric vehicle jointly developed by British carmaker Jaguar Land Rover and Chinese joint-venture partner Chery displayed at a launch event in Wuhu, China. Photograph: Nick Carey/Reuters

Flagship UK gigafactory plan in turmoil after it loses second builder in five months

Tata-owned Agratas plant to build EV batteries for sister company Jaguar Land Rover seen as crucial for long-term health of British car industry

One of the UK’s flagship electric vehicle battery projects has been thrown into turmoil after its second building contractor in five months walked away, adding to questions over when Jaguar Land Rover cars will use British-made batteries.

The £5.2bn gigafactory in Bridgwater, Somerset, is being built by Agratas, to provide batteries for Britain’s largest automotive employer, its sister company. Agratas and Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) are both part of Indian conglomerate Tata Group.

The UK government has pledged £380m in financial support for the factory because it is seen as crucial to the long-term survival of the British car industry, but the build has suffered several setbacks. The construction specialist contracted by Agratas, TSL, has decided to leave the project after failing to agree terms with Agratas, according to three sources.

Batteries are among the important parts of EVs, but global supply is now dominated by China, South Korea and Japan. Successive Conservative and Labour governments have strongly supported efforts to build a British battery supply chain, and it also fits with Andy Burnham’s hopes to “reindustrialise” the UK. Not all of the subsidy has yet been paid out.

items.title: Asylum seekers removed from UK subjected to ‘unnecessary and intimidating’ force
items.summary: Incidents include suicidal man being carried on to plane in waist, leg and ankle restraints, official report says “Unnecessary and intimidating” behaviour was used against asylum seekers being deported under the UK’s controversial “one in, one out” scheme, including a vulnerable person being carried…
items.body:
Twenty-six use-of-force incidents were recorded on Home Office deportation charter flights between July and September 2026. Photograph: Mike Kemp/Getty Images/Tetra images RF

Twenty-six use-of-force incidents were recorded on Home Office deportation charter flights between July and September 2026. Photograph: Mike Kemp/Getty Images/Tetra images RF

Asylum seekers removed from UK subjected to ‘unnecessary and intimidating’ force

Incidents include suicidal man being carried on to plane in waist, leg and ankle restraints, official report says

“Unnecessary and intimidating” behaviour was used against asylum seekers being deported under the UK’s controversial “one in, one out” scheme, including a vulnerable person being carried on to a flight in restraints, according to a report.

Many of those deported to France under the scheme – which involved one asylum seeker who arrived in the UK in a small boat being forcibly returned to France in exchange for another in northern France brought legally to the UK to claim asylum – have fled conflict zones and are survivors of torture or trafficking.

According to freedom of information data shared with the Guardian about Home Office deportation charter flights between July and September 2026, 26 use-of-force incidents were recorded on 26 deportation charters – 21 to France and the others to Albania, Lithuania and Romania. Not every deportation flight involved a use-of-force incident.

After reviewing body-worn footage of four previous deportation flights to France the HM inspectorate of prisons team identified nine incidents of use of force, at least one that was not formally recorded by escorts. Monday’s HMIP report looked specifically at the deportation charter flight to France on 4 September.

‘Signs of violence’: asylum seekers arriving in France injured after being deported from UK

Read more

In the case of the three documented use-of-force incidents on the flight, one man described by inspectors as “fragile”, who was not eating consistently, posed no threat and had no history of active resistance or violence, was taken from his cell by staff in full protective gear including helmets and riot shields and was placed in a waist restraint belt and leg restraints, even though he had not resisted. Techniques to carry him out were found to be “poorly applied” and “disproportionate”. During the flight he “remained slumped and non-communicative”.

In a second case a man who was on constant suicide watch was carried out to the plane in a waist restraint belt, along with leg and ankle restraints. In a third case a man was placed in a waist restraint belt because he said he was not going to comply with his removal.

The Guardian has previously highlighted concerns about the state in which one in, one out asylum seekers were being returned to France. A report from Samusocial de Paris, which was commissioned by one of France’s regional health agencies to provide healthcare to returned asylum seekers, found: “Consultations are revealing signs consistent with recent physical and psychological violence as well as the consequences of prolonged detention in conditions described as particularly degrading.”

It states that the physical and psychological conditions documented are “explicitly linked to the implementation of the France-British agreement”.

The HMIP report said inspectors “mostly observed caring and respectful interactions” but also found that leadership of collection teams was “not always active enough to address some unnecessary and intimidating behaviour”.

A bodyworn video camera that doubled as an interpreting tool was found not to work effectively and many asylum seekers were unable to access either adequate interpretation or lawyers to represent them.

Inspectors also found that the asylum seekers were referred to by numbers rather than by their names and that those taken to the plane by van were given bags to urinate into.

The Guardian reported in November that despite the scheme ending in October, there were still incidences of people being removed.

Emma Ginn, director of the charity Medical Justice, said: “This report’s findings come as no surprise. Medical Justice has long evidenced the severe and avoidable harm of the government’s dehumanising mistreatment of vulnerable people during immigration enforcement – it cannot be described it as accidental.

“Our independent clinicians assessed that most of our clients detained under the one in, one out scheme had clinical evidence of torture. It should be a source of shame that torture survivors have been mistreated and retraumatised in UK immigration removal centres and while being deported back to France having suffered additional severe harm here.”

The Home Office has been approached from comment.

items.summary: Former US vice-president Al Gore among climate leaders demanding change to consensus rule after Antalya summit The failure at Cop31 to reach a keystone agreement has exposed the need to reform how the UN’s climate summits make decisions, say international climate diplomacy experts and scientists. Th…
items.body:
Al Gore speaking during Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, this month. Photograph: Chris McGrath/Getty Images

Al Gore speaking during Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, this month. Photograph: Chris McGrath/Getty Images

Failure of Cop31 prompts calls for urgent reform of UN climate summits

Former US vice-president Al Gore among climate leaders demanding change to consensus rule after Antalya summit

The failure at Cop31 to reach a keystone agreement has exposed the need to reform how the UN’s climate summits make decisions, say international climate diplomacy experts and scientists.

The talks in Antalya, co-chaired by Turkey and Australia, were supposed to agree a sweeping pact that would have injected urgency into calls for climate action around the world and support for countries exposed to the crisis.

Cop31 failed but in ‘the real world’ the transition away from fossil fuels is inevitable

Read more

But because decisions at summits can only be made by consensus, the “Antalya pact” was stopped in its tracks at the final plenary meeting, after countries became entrenched. Faced with the final draft of the cover decision, many were angry it did not “meet the moment” of the climate crisis, nor even mention the words “fossil fuels” – an omission seen as a sop to petrostates.

The former US vice-president and climate activist Al Gore said the failure at Cop31 was an outrage and significant reform was needed. “World leaders no longer want to settle for the lowest common denominator. They want real action to implement and finance a just transition away from fossil fuels. It has been clear for years that the Cop process is in need of significant reform,” he said.

He said most countries had come to Antalya to move forward “in good faith” and it was “time that we empower those leaders with a reinvigorated multilateral process that reflects the latest science and represents the will of the majority of the world”.

EU officials reject Cop31 deal as it 'doesn't speak to reality of the climate crisis' – video

In the moments after the pact died, the Australian climate minister, Chris Bowen, co-chair of Cop31, said: “The fundamental root problem is that when Cops were created, for reasons I understand, it was made consensus only. That’s a very tough ask when you also need consensus to change consensus, which is a particular challenge.” He said there had been at attempt at Cop31 to introduce efficiency reforms.

The UN’s chief climate negotiator, Simon Stiell, defended the consensus-based approach, saying it had succeeded with the 2015 Paris agreement, helping to lower expected global heating at the end of the century from almost 5C to 2.6C. But as the talks wound up, he conceded the consensus system had fallen short in Antalya.

skip past newsletter promotion

after newsletter promotion

Cop31 left Chris Bowen stuck between petrostates and climate reality. But the f-word failure is not his alone

Read more

Stiell said he was championing a review process within the UN climate convention to seek external advice on “areas of potential reform”.

Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said Cops needed to transition from “negotiating promises and commitments that we never deliver on” to a focus on accountability for promises made and their implementation.

Tobias Holle, the co-founder of the NGO group Shifting Advocacy, said Cop31 and previous failures “show that the process is not fit for purpose any more”. He said: “Despite the political will of the many, the few blocking the progress end

up winning in a process whose rules and decision-making structures repeatedly allow the lowest common denominator to dictate the level of ambition. We need a structural reform that delivers on climate justice.”

Cop31’s big fossil fuel failure – podcast

Read more

During the talks, Panama released an open letter to the Cop co-chairs on areas on which it would refuse to compromise during negotiations, including that a path be opened up to changing from consensus to simple majority voting.

Matt McDonald, a professor of international relations at the University of Queensland in Australia, who was at the talks, said: “The legacy of Cop31 might be recognition of the limits of this consensus-driven approach to climate negotiations and the development of alternative sites for climate action.”

He said it was “a different world now” than in 2015 when the Paris agreement was forged, “raising questions about the future of this type of consensus-based multilateralism going forward”.

Cop31 overran its official end-time of Friday evening, ending late on Sunday, making it the longest climate summit so far. It was also, according to many estimates, the largest.

The decision by countries including those in the EU bloc, Panama, Belize, Vanuatu, the UK, the Marshall Islands and Norway to formally object to the cover decision meant the pact could not be gavelled through. Some view the outcome as a positive decision to walk away – a “sign of courage”, as the former UN climate chief Christiana Figueres has called it.

China, India and a large number of developing countries did not formally object to the text and subsequently expressed their disappointment at the failure of the pact. The Ghana delegation, which accepted the text, told the plenary: “Africa has always chosen to build multilateralism rather than walk away from it.”

items.title: Arctic air brings colder temperatures to Europe this week
items.summary: After a warmer-than-average November so far globally, a cold snap is on the horizon in parts of Europe While average global temperatures continue to set records through one of the strongest El Niños on record, temperatures across a large swathe of Europe could plunge this week, as Arctic air sweeps…
items.body:
People on the Charles Bridge in Prague, Czechia, in 2022. As low pressure pushes into western and central Europe, significant snow is expected this week. Photograph: Petr David Josek/AP

People on the Charles Bridge in Prague, Czechia, in 2022. As low pressure pushes into western and central Europe, significant snow is expected this week. Photograph: Petr David Josek/AP

Arctic air brings colder temperatures to Europe this week

After a warmer-than-average November so far globally, a cold snap is on the horizon in parts of Europe

While average global temperatures continue to set records through one of the strongest El Niños on record, temperatures across a large swathe of Europe could plunge this week, as Arctic air sweeps in.

On Friday, the global average temperature was 2.12C higher than the preindustrial average, the biggest ever anomaly and equivalent to 1.22C above the 1991-2020 climate average.

But in parts of Europe, high pressure building over Scandinavia and low pressure shifting south-east into western Russia will open a corridor of cold air from the north. Temperatures in the Baltics and in countries such as Germany, Poland and Ukraine are likely to fall widely below zero from Monday, with ice days – in which temperatures stay below 0C all day – expected from midweek. By the weekend, temperatures could be 5-15C below average, reaching double-digit negatives on higher ground.

The low pressure over eastern Europe and western Russia will bring extensive snowfall. Southern Poland, Belarus, eastern Ukraine and south-eastern parts of the Baltics will be the first to see widespread snow, which could reach up to 10cm in southern Poland.

Temperatures are expected to fall below zero in Germany, Austria and Czechia. Photograph: Peeradon Warithkorasuth/Getty Images

Later in the week, as a smaller area of low pressure pushes into western and central Europe, significant snow is expected to spread across southern Germany, Austria and Czechia, where depths of 10-20cm could build. The Alps could get a significant dumping of snow, a welcome boost for the region’s ski resorts which will open in the coming weeks.

Into the weekend and the start of December, high pressure is set to remain dominant across northern Europe, maintaining below-average temperatures in central and eastern Europe and possibly extending into the Balkans. There are also hints that the sudden stratospheric warming earlier this month could finally begin influencing the lower atmosphere, with high pressure extending farther west and perhaps bringing cold easterly winds into western Europe and the UK, although confidence on this is low.

The cold in Europe is in stark contrast to the global picture. This October was the warmest on record, with an average global temperature of 15.35C, 0.9C above the 1991-2020 average and 1.75C above the estimated preindustrial level. It was the third month in a row above 1.5C, following August and September, and while parts of Europe, including the UK, have seen below-average temperatures so far this November, global temperatures this month have continued to run above average.

There are also hints that the sudden stratospheric warming earlier this month could finally begin influencing the lower atmosphere, with high pressure extending farther west and perhaps bringing cold easterly winds into western Europe and the UK, although confidence on this is low.

The cold in Europe is in stark contrast to the global picture. This October was the warmest on record, with an average global temperature of 15.35C, 0.9C above the 1991-2020 average and 1.75C above the estimated preindustrial level. items.title: Israeli attacks have turned Gaza into 'toxic wasteland', Oxfam says
items.summary: The report says there are signs of possible contamination across almost all of Gaza as a result of Israel's actions.
items.body:
Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images

Image caption,

The UN estimates that Israeli forces dropped more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives on Gaza in almost two years (file photo)

ByYolande Knell

Middle East correspondent, Reporting fromJerusalem

Gaza has been turned into "a toxic wasteland", with more than 99% of the Palestinian territory showing indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks, a new report from the non-profit organisation Oxfam says, external.

Heavy metals, explosive residues, and asbestos from destroyed buildings, dioxins and biological contaminants in the air, soil and water supply are threats to Palestinians now and potentially for decades to come, it says.

Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, accuses Israel of "environmental war crimes" as part of an "ongoing genocide in Gaza."

"The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival," he says.

Israel's government has been asked for its response to the report.

It has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted. Israel maintains that its military campaign in Gaza is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.

Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images

Image caption,

The report says 99% of Gaza shows indicators of potential environmental contamination

Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data to draw their conclusions in the most comprehensive report to date on the severe environmental impacts caused by three years of intense war in Gaza.

The report details how munitions used in Israel's intense bombardment, as well as the debris from destroyed buildings and infrastructure, all have an impact on the environment. In February, a UN special rapporteur stated that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years - "the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs".

Last year, the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) estimated that Israel's military operations destroying homes and infrastructure had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris across the territory, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of contamination from hazardous materials.

"There are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment," Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC.

She says that now and in future Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.

Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Only a small fraction of the more than 60 million tonnes of debris in Gaza has been cleared

With all six wastewater treatment plants out of operation in Gaza, untreated sewage currently makes its way into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea. The health impact has recently been exacerbated by heavy winter storms causing rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people.

Testing types and levels of contamination is often not possible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and there are Israeli restrictions on the entry of specialist testing equipment and scientists. The BBC has approached the Israeli military for comment.

UNEP said security concerns also prevented its expert staff from previously travelling to Gaza.

The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to be carried out in Gaza to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up. It says special attention must be given to the protection of workers involved.

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

Recent winter storms caused rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent camps

Already, Gazan doctors have been reporting increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard to keep warm and cook food. Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation.

A Palestinian dermatologist, Dr Alaa Abu Hajar, told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war, putting this down to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic living conditions in tents and displacement camps.

"There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets," he says. "Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children."

Image caption,

Dr Alaa Abu Hajar has seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the start of the war

Farmers and those working in fishing say that pollution of the soil and sea mean they are unable to produce food that is safe.

"Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster," complains fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan. "There is also rubble from destroyed houses that's dumped into the sea. When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage. This harms the marine environment; the fish are affected and so are the fishermen."

At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says that humanitarian conditions remain dire.

Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. In July, Hamas accepted a plan put forward by the US-led Board of Peace to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal. However, the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

items.body:
The high street retailer said its own systems had not been compromised by the hack. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

The high street retailer said its own systems had not been compromised by the hack. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

Next issues cyber-attack warning after ‘benign’ data accessed by hackers

Retailer says it believes no personal data that could lead to fraud was accessed after hack of third-party supplier

• Business live – latest updates

Next has warned that hackers have gained access to data relating to the clothing and homewares retailer through a technology supplier.

The firm said on Monday that it had been informed that one of its third-party suppliers had “experienced a cyber incident” resulting in unauthorised access to the data.

The high street chain said it believed that customers’ personal data had not been compromised and the information affected was “limited in nature and, based on our current assessment, cannot be used to facilitate fraud against our customers or Next”.

It is understood the data accessed does not include information such as contact details, addresses, passwords or bank details, which could be used to commit fraud.

It said Next’s systems had not been compromised, though it was “affecting the supplier’s environment” in its business.

Investigations into the hack are in progress. Next said in a statement to investors: “Despite the limited and benign nature of the affected data, we are treating the matter with the utmost seriousness and are working closely with the supplier, law enforcement and relevant regulatory authorities.”

The latest incident comes amid a spate of cyber-attacks against high-profile retailers around the world.

Last week it emerged that a secret UK government cybersecurity operation had warded off the risk of a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums.

That came after hackers caused many millions of euros of damage in continental Europe, with attacks on fridge and freezer control systems in recent months.

Fashion retailers including the owner of Hobbs and Whistles, TFG London, and the online fashion seller Asos have faced cyber-attacks in which customer data was accessed.

Last year, several other British retailers, including Marks & Spencer, the Co-op and Harrods, were hit by damaging cyber incidents which affected operations for months.

items.summary: Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship Europe live – latest updates Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Ru…
items.body:
Onboard view of maritime drone approaching vessel off Benghazi on Sunday. Photograph: Volodymyr Zelenskyy/Telegram/Reuters

Onboard view of maritime drone approaching vessel off Benghazi on Sunday. Photograph: Volodymyr Zelenskyy/Telegram/Reuters

Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya

Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship

• Europe live – latest updates

Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.

Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.

“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.

Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.

locator map

In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”

Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.

The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hitthe Kerch bridge - a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic sea port of Kaliningrad.

Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.

Large blaze at Benghazi port after suspected drone attack on Russian warship – video

Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.

At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.

Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.

Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.

More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, the Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base in the to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.

The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli said in a statement it was alarmed by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.

There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”

Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.

In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.

Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.

Image source, Planet Labs PBC

Image caption,

Satellite imagery showed a ship on fire early on Sunday morning

ByHafsa Khalil

Updated 4 minutes ago

An explosion has occurred on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port after a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.

The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government.

It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.

Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged.

Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark.

The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.

Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.

GNS said the country was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.

Seperately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.

GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".

Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.

items.body: More than two weeks of talks in Turkey fail to produce a resolution to tackle climate crisis. Plus, a savage review of Melania’s new documentary Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here Good morning. The world’s nations have failed to reach agreement at the Cop31 talks in Turkey. In a dramatic conclusion to the summit, major powers rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels. The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien. What was in the proposed agreement? The Antalya pact invited nations to electrify their economies, called on wealthy countries to fund climate adaptation for poorer ones, and urged signatories to minimise any “overshoot” of the Paris agreement’s 1.5C global heating threshold. However, it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” demanded by more than 130 countries, instead including controversial provisions on carbon capture and storage technology that critics argued would perpetuate fossil fuel use. What precipitated the collapse of the talks? In this analysis piece , the Guardian’s environment editor, who was at Cop, explains that after a marathon negotiating session ran more than 40 hours past its deadline, a small group led by Saudi Arabia refused to accept any mention of a “transition away from fossil fuels”. While such holdouts would normally force through a watered-down compromise, nearly 40 nations – led by the EU, the UK, small islands and least developed countries – broke with precedent and openly rejected the weakened text, refusing to salvage the usual face-saving semblance of unity. items.summary: Brian Morales García of Texas seeks damages after he was wrongly identified as undocumented in case White House wants dropped The Trump administration recently admitted in federal court that it deported a US citizen to Mexico after American authorities incorrectly concluded he was an undocumented im…
items.body:

Court filings recount how border patrol agent Robert Gil Jr consulted records from Mexico that listed a Mexican birthplace for Brian Morales. Photograph: Dominic Gwinn/Middle East Images/AFP/Getty Images

Trump administration deported US citizen to Mexico, DoJ admits in court

Brian Morales García of Texas seeks damages after he was wrongly identified as undocumented in case White House wants dropped

The Trump administration recently admitted in federal court that it deported a US citizen to Mexico after American authorities incorrectly concluded he was an undocumented immigrant.

Attorneys for the US justice department made that admission on Friday while requesting the dismissal of a lawsuit for damages that the deported man – Brian José Morales García of Austin, Texas – has been pursuing against the federal government.

Morales García’s case took that turn as the White House has faced bipartisan criticism for the aggressive mass deportation campaign pursued by Donald Trump throughout his second presidency – widely seen as a factor in the electoral battering his Republican party suffered during the 3 November midterms, costing it control of Congress.

The Denver-born, Mexico-raised Morales García was riding with his boss to his job as an air-conditioning installation technician on 3 April when they were pulled over by state and local officers near Fredericksburg, Texas.

They went out to celebrate at a Memphis bar. Then, ICE descended

Read more

Morales García was his boss’s passenger and did not have his identification on him. The 25-year-old also told the officers that he had his birth certificate and social security card at home, but they didn’t believe him – so they called immigration agents, who detained Morales García.

Court filings recount how Robert Gil Jr, a US Customs and Border Protection agent, consulted records from Mexico that listed a Mexican birthplace for Morales García. Gil Jr also accused Morales García of saying he was born in Mexico and observed that he only spoke in Spanish, according to court records.

Morales García was deported on 7 April, with the Trump administration later accusing him in a media statement of being in the country illegally.

Morales García’s attorneys sued on 1 May, maintaining that he had falsely said he entered the US illegally and signed papers for a rapid deportation in response to threats of imprisonment by agents. His lawsuit, which seeks an unspecified amount of money, also contended that family and friends tried to deliver documents proving his US citizenship before this deportation.

But those efforts were unduly rebuffed, Morales García’s lawsuit said.

The Trump administration denied Morales García’s assertions, saying on Friday that he went to Mexico voluntarily and therefore lacked any basis to sue the federal government for damages. Nonetheless, in court filings on Friday, the administration conceded that Morales García “was permitted entry” back into the US on 30 August after it reviewed “information concerning plaintiff’s place of birth”.

“Plaintiff is a dual citizen of the United States and Mexico,” Justin Simmons, the US attorney for the western district of Texas, wrote in a court filing first reported by the Texas Tribune.

Judge says ICE ‘made a mockery of court orders’ with instant re-arrest policy

Read more

Americans are not required to carry proof of citizenship when going about their daily business. Lawyers across the US have seen cases such as Morales García’s, which begin after an encounter with local authorities demonstrate how those officials are generally not aware of the nuances of immigration policy.

Texas’s public safety department is among many US state and local agencies that collaborate with federal immigration authorities under their 287(g) program.

The judge presiding over Morales García’s lawsuit, Robert Lee Pitman, did not immediately rule on the Trump administration’s request on Friday to dismiss the case. The lawsuit also named unspecified local and state Texas law enforcement officers as defendants.

An October 2025 report by ProPublica found that immigration agents had detained more than 170 US citizens during the first nine months of Trump’s second presidency.

Meanwhile, the media statement incorrectly saying Morales García was in the US illegally is among several related to immigration enforcement under the Trump administration that has unraveled under scrutiny.

A Guardian analysis published in July reviewed Trump administration press releases on 26 cases of cars allegedly being used to assault immigration enforcement agents – and nearly all were either disproven or dropped.

items.body:
It is proposed that visitor numbers will be limited to between 600 and 1,000 a day in June to September. Photograph: Nicolas Escobar/Getty Images

It is proposed that visitor numbers will be limited to between 600 and 1,000 a day in June to September. Photograph: Nicolas Escobar/Getty Images

Chamonix mayor plans tourist limits for Alpine beauty spot

Rising numbers around Lac Blanc are having big impact on environment and on visitors’ enjoyment, mayor says

In the Alpine town of Chamonix, most tourist paths lead to the national park with spectacular views across Mont Blanc and the shrinking blue glaciers. In the summer, up to 4,000 tourists a day hike or take the cable car to the lakes high in the Aiguilles Rouges nature reserve.

Many of them descend disappointed. Once a place of nature and tranquility, the beauty spot’s visitor numbers have more than doubled since 2020, spoiling the experience and leaving trails of litter, threatening the environment and wildlife.

Now Chamonix plans to become the first town in the Alps to introduce visitor quotas, to limit the number of hikers around Lac Blanc and the Lacs des Chéserys.

The town’s mayor, Francois-Xavier Laffin, announced last week that from next June tourists would be required to book in advance to visit the area. After booking, they will receive a QR code granting them access.

People visit the ice cave of the Mer de Glace glacier in Chamonix. Photograph: Delpixart/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Laffin championed the quotas after visiting Marseille, where a similar scheme was introduced limiting access to the Calanques national park in 2022. He said the aim was “reserve to preserve”, adding that visiting the mountains would still be free but subject to conditions.

Laffin said mass tourism was having a major impact on the environment, wildlife and on visitors’ enjoyment of the reserve. “Lac Blanc is one place we cannot let continue to deteriorate” he said, adding that the council was looking at additional regulations in other areas.

The plan, which needs the final approval of the local prefect, would restrict the number of visitors to the Lac Blanc area to between 600 and 1,000 a day for four months from June to September.

Christian Schwoehrer, the director of the Haute-Savoie Nature Conservation Agency, which manages the reserve, said: “We will see how it works for the next three years and if it does then it will be extended and maybe applied to other areas. This is a nature reserve but when there are thousands of visitors a day there’s no peace for the protected species or local people and we need stronger measures to control this.

“At points of entry [to the reserve] there will be ‘eco guards’ to verify that people have reserved. If they haven’t, they could be fined, though our intention is to avoid fining people by making sure they know in advance and cannot say they weren’t warned.”

Visitors near Lac Blanc in the Aiguilles Rouge nature reserve above Chamonix. Photograph: Simon Turner/Alamy

The quota plan has met some local opposition from the land’s legal owners. Lac Blanc sits in just under 3 square miles of private estate held by 35 families under a historic entity that has existed for centuries and is now managed by the Montagne de Chéserys company.

One of the landowners, Guillaume Ravanel, a mountain guide, agreed tourist numbers need controlling but suggested visitors should be asked to pay a small entry fee to access the reserve.

Frédéric Charlet-Berguerand, a co-manager of Montagne de Chéserys, told Le Monde: “This quota system is innovative and virtuous.” Contacted by the Guardian, he added: “That said, there will be no quotas on our private property until they are approved by a meeting of the owners,” due to be held in December. “Let’s not put the cart before the horse.”

The mayor is also looking at tighter controls on the Ultra-Trail du Mont Blanc. Photograph: AscentXmedia/Getty Images

Laffin said the quota plan would cost about €590,000 for the three-year “experimental” period. Financing has yet to be arranged but he said part would be raised by Chamonix and other local authorities and the town would be applying for a grant from the government’s “green fund” to help protect the environment. Private sponsors are also being sought.

The mayor, elected in March, has made managing tourist numbers a priority. He is also looking at tighter controls on the three-week Ultra-Trail du Mont Blanc, an ultramarathon circling the Mont-Blanc massif through France, Italy and Switzerland that begins in Chamonix. The event, started in 2003, now attracts 10,000 runners and up to 50,000 visitors each August.

Schwoehrer said summer crowds meant local people were avoiding the reserve. A recent survey found that 55% of visitors who ascended to Lac Blanc said they were disappointed by the experience, he said.

“We don’t want to stop people going there, just have a few stronger rules. It’s a compromise to ensure that visitors have a good experience and at the same time the natural environment is protected.”

items.body: Party that won just 0.2% of the vote in 2016 is on course for almost 20% this time and could be part of next government Almost exactly eight years ago, a video clip of a stocky, bearded man riding a horse through western Andalucía went viral in Spain . The rider was Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, the soundtrack was a bombastic snatch of the Lord of the Rings score, and the caption was an equally unsubtle callback to the 700-year fight to wrest the Iberian peninsula from Islamic rule. “La Reconquista comenzará en tierras andaluzas,” it read – the reconquest will begin on Andalucían soil. Celebrated by some, jeered by others – and inventively lampooned by those with sufficient skill and time on their hands – the video didn’t seem quite as amusing three weeks later when Vox broke through into the political mainstream by winning 12 seats in Andalucía’s regional parliament.
